steps.intro: Greek words carry small marks above and beside their letters. Listen for what each one changes as you read these aloud.

cards.en: the word (the mark ‘ on ὁ adds an h)
day (h again, then stress on ME)
word, saying (ῥ at the start of a word, like English rh in rhythm)

cards.title: Breathing marks: is there an h?
body: Every word that begins with a vowel has a breathing mark over it. ῾ (rough breathing, like an opening quote) means say an h first. ᾿ (smooth breathing, like an apostrophe) means no h.

When a word begins with a pair of vowels, the mark sits on the second one: οὐρανός, εἰμί, υἱός. A word beginning with ρ or υ always takes the rough breathing, which is why English has rhythm and hydro-.

cards.title: Accents: which syllable to stress
body: Most words carry one accent. In the pronunciation used here, all three simply mark the stressed syllable: acute ´, grave ` and circumflex ῀.
A grave usually replaces an acute on the last syllable when another word follows: καί on its own, but καὶ in a sentence. It is the same word.
Sometimes the accent is the only difference between two words, so it is worth noticing.

cards.title: Little marks with a job
body: A small ι written under α, η or ω (ᾳ ῃ ῳ) is called iota subscript. It isn't sounded, but it matters for grammar, as you'll see with nouns.
Two dots over a vowel (¨) mean it starts a new syllable: Ἠσαΐας is ay-sa-EE-as (Isaiah).
An apostrophe shows a dropped vowel before another vowel: δι’ αὐτοῦ is διά αὐτοῦ, through him.

examples.en: in the beginning (ι under η, not sounded)

cards.title: Punctuation and capitals
body: Full stops and commas look and work as in English. A raised dot (·) is a pause like a colon or semicolon. And the Greek question mark is ; — a semicolon in English eyes.

Capital letters mark names and the start of a paragraph, not every sentence. There are no quotation marks either: a raised dot often comes just before someone's words, as in λέγει αὐτοῖς· (he says to them:).

cards.prompt: Which word begins with an h sound?
cards.explain: ἡμέρα has the rough breathing ῾ : hay-ME-ra. The others have the smooth breathing ᾿ : no h.

cards.prompt: In οὐρανός the breathing mark sits on υ, not ο. Why?
options: ου is one sound, and the mark goes on the second vowel
it shows where to stress the word
cards.explain: With a pair of vowels the breathing (and any accent) goes on the second vowel.

cards.prompt: A Greek sentence ends with ; — what does that mean?
Which syllable do you stress in ἄνθρωπος (person)?
cards.explain: The accent sits on ἄ, so stress the first syllable. Anthropology comes from this word.

cards.prompt: Match each mark to what it tells you.
Describe the marks on ᾧ (to whom).
cards.explain: ᾧ is said hoh: the rough breathing gives the h, the circumflex marks the stress, and the ι underneath is written but not sounded.

steps.intro: Read these aloud, watching the marks: h sounds, stressed syllables and punctuation.

cards.note: Spot the raised dot after αὐτοῖς (“he says to them:”) and the question mark at the end: “But who do you say that I am?”
δι’ αὐτοῦ is διά with its last vowel dropped: “all things came into being through him”.
